newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr tone hardens as yield spreads widen.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr tone hardens as yield spreads widen.

text.p: The Australian dollar absorbed last minute profit-taking Friday to end the week a cent firmer and well placed to extend its rally short term.

Traders said the selling came largely from U.S. banks but was countered around US$0.7830 support by demand from exporters and Tokyo, with the latter keen to buy A$ government bonds and dual currency samurais following a widening in yield spreads.

There was some disappointment amongst bulls that retail sales data today were not emphatic enough to completely rule out another official easing, but dealers felt the risk of a cut had diminished and this should underpin the A$ for now.

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the currency was making itself at home at US$0.7831/36 having drifted from an early US$0.7835/40 and US$0.7847/52 late here Thursday. This was still its best weekly close since April 11 and 1/2 cent up on last Friday's finish.

Traders said offers had been thick around US$0.7860 chart resistance this morning, perhaps related to much rumoured options position, and the currency never came close to the crucial technical target at US$0.7890/7905.
Support was seen at US$0.7830 and US$0.7795 with the Japanese noteable buyers, partly for a 25 billion yen dual currency samurai bond, the fourth such issue of the week.

This interest helped keep the dollar up at 99.12/22 after it ran into offshore profit taking on topping 100.00 yen Thursday for the first time since May 1992. In trade weighted terms it edged down to 60.9 from 61.1, well up on last weeek's 60.4.
There was also talk of possible offshore buying related to the sale of three Federal airports which are rumoured to be worth a total A$3.0 billion.

Two of the bidding consortium do include foreign companies, suggesting a need for A$ might exist, but their partners were large Australian institutions and dealers felt much of the money needed would be raised here.

Data on domestic retail sales proved a touch softer than expected with a fall of 0.3 percent against forecasts of a flat result, which disappointed some bulls who had hoped for a strong enough result to extinguish all thoughts of another easing.

Nevertheless, real sales were still up a healthy 2.2 percent on the quarter and promised to add 0.5 point to GDP growth. Coming on top of unexpectedly ronbust wages growth, it was enough to convince analysts a rate cut unlikely this month.
The RBA's board holds its monthly policy meeting Tuesday and there had been some speculation it might take advantage of low inflation to ease policy and give employment a fillip.
"The sales data reinforce the view that the RBA would be unwise to adjust monetary policy at the board meeting," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"Coming on top of the wages data and signs of further expansion in privarte sector housing and car sales, there are no compelling reasons to cut rates," he said.

Nevertheless, the talk might yet revive if jobs data on Thursday are weak again, so the market will be cautious until then. Median forecasts are for employment to bounce back by 35,000 in April after falling 33,900 the month before, but at least one analyst saw a risk of a negative number.

In contrast benign U.S. employment cost data this week had made the market re-assess its expectations for how much the Federal Reserve would have to tighten this year -- so much so that it shrugged off a whopping 5.6 percent rise in Q1 U.S. GDP reported on Wednesday.
That diversion of opinion had seen Asutralian yields rise sharply while U.S. rates fell and made A$/US$ spreads favour the former again.
Analysts cautioned that the trend may accelerate, or even reverse, depending on U.S. non-farm payrolls tonight.
